name: Uma Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a herd hand on Calloway's, a dairy farm with about a hundred and eighty cows, black and white Holsteins mostly. Alarm goes at four, I'm in the parlour by half past, that's the milking shed, and I'm putting clusters on teats till about seven. Then it's scraping out the cubicle passages, feeding the calves, bedding, and back in the parlour for the afternoon milking at three.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the calves. There's one I named Biscuit who follows me down the pen like a dog. What wears me out is the hours, honestly, and that I'm still slow. Glen, the owner, can spot a cow coming down with mastitis, that's an infection in the udder, from across the yard, and I still miss them.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Where do you live, and who's at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Me and my partner Tom live in the farm cottage at the end of the lane. It comes with the job, which is good because the rent's low, and bad because if the job goes, the house goes. Tom drives a delivery van for a parcel firm in town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, leave it as a search engine. I don't use any of that stuff anyway. Tom's got a chatbot thing on his phone and he asks it recipes, and that's about as far as it goes in our house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means nothing changes, and nothing changing isn't brilliant either. I'm on the lowest rate Glen can pay, and I've got about three weeks of money in the bank. But at least I know where I stand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as every year. Try to get the dairy course done at the college, the one-day-a-week one Glen keeps mentioning, so I can do the AI breeding. Not that AI, I mean artificial insemination, putting the cows in calf. Funny, that's the only AI I'll ever touch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Boring, but fine. It's the version where I just keep getting up at four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the course. What's stopped you doing it so far?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money, and nerves a bit. The course is free but I'd lose a day's pay a week unless Glen covers it, and he's not said he would. And I left school at sixteen, so a classroom makes my stomach turn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you could change one thing about the job in this picture, what would it be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pay, straight away. I think anybody who milks cows twice a day, Christmas included, should be in a union and have a proper rate set. There's no union on our farm, there's three of us, so who would even run it?

S0.say: I'd tell people to leave it as a search engine, because I don't use any of it anyway. In my house the most it does is help Tom find a recipe.
S0.think: Privately I think nothing changing isn't great either, because I'm on the lowest rate and have about three weeks of money saved. At least it's a version where I know where I stand.
S0.do: Keeps getting up at four and keeps milking. Tries to start the one-day-a-week dairy course so she can learn artificial insemination, though losing a day's pay makes that hard.
S0.feel: Settled but flat. It's the version where she just keeps going, which is safe but not hopeful.
S0.quote: Not that AI, I mean artificial insemination, putting the cows in calf. Funny, that's the only AI I'll ever touch.
S0.fieldNote: She joked about the other kind of AI straight away, which set the tone: technology is something that happens in other people's houses. Her real anchor is the tied cottage, mentioned before I'd even asked about money. Wants a union but sees no way to build one on a three-person farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say, that they should be hiring more young ones into farming, not fewer. Half the people I went to school with won't go near a farm because the pay's rubbish. If companies stop taking beginners, who's going to milk in twenty years?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm the beginner. I'm below average, I know that, Glen knows that. If the next Glen decides one good herdsman and a bit of tech is cheaper than a slow girl who's still learning, that's me finished, and the cottage with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and work harder, I suppose. Turn up early, stop moaning about weekends. Maybe finally do that course so I'm not the cheapest one to drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like when you hear a cow coughing in the night and you don't know which one it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stop moaning about weekends. What would you be giving up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sunday afternoons. Glen lets me off every other Sunday after morning milking, and that's when Tom and I go to his mum's for dinner. I'd probably offer to do them, just to look keen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think would decide whether beginners get hired?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not Glen, really. The milk buyer, the big dairy that takes our milk, pays what it likes and Glen just has to swallow it. So when he's squeezed, he squeezes us. I'd blame the dairy and the supermarkets behind it before I'd blame him.

S1.say: I'd say they should be hiring more young people into farming, not fewer. If companies stop taking beginners, nobody will be left to milk the cows in twenty years.
S1.think: I'm the beginner they'd stop hiring, and I know I'm below average. If a boss decides one good herdsman plus some tech is cheaper than me, I lose the job and the cottage together.
S1.do: Works harder and offers to cover her free Sunday afternoons to look keen. Tries again to start the dairy course so she isn't the cheapest worker to let go.
S1.feel: Uneasy, with a worry she can't quite place. She feels watched rather than threatened.
S1.quote: Off the record, I'm the beginner. I'm below average, I know that, Glen knows that.
S1.fieldNote: Her public line is about the industry; her private line is about herself, and she was blunt about her own skill. She blames the milk buyer and supermarkets rather than her boss, which fits her left-leaning view. Her plan is effort, not learning anything new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd say that's the office lot's problem, and I'd feel a bit bad saying it. I'd be on the side of the people losing jobs, though. I'd sign the petitions, I'd say tax the companies doing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's a bit of a relief. There's no office on our farm, just Glen's wife Maureen doing the books at the kitchen table. Nobody's sending a robot to scrape cubicles because of a computer program.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably nothing different on the farm. Tom might be the one to worry, because if the parcel firm puts AI on the routes and cuts drivers' hours, we're down to my wage. I'd check what the cheapest phone deal is and cancel the streaming, that kind of thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sorry for them, safe for me. Bit guilty about feeling safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Tom. What would happen at home if his hours got cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd be in trouble by the second month. My wage covers the cottage and the food, his covers the car, the phones and anything nice. We'd sell his motorbike first. He'd hate that, he's had it since he was nineteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd sign petitions. What would you actually want politicians to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Make the companies that save money pay into something for the people they let go. Proper retraining, paid while you do it. Not some website where you click through videos.

S2.say: I'd say it's mostly the office workers' problem, but I'd be on their side. I'd sign the petitions and say the companies doing the layoffs should be taxed for it.
S2.think: Privately it's a bit of a relief, because the only office on our farm is Glen's wife doing the books at the kitchen table. Nobody replaces a cubicle scraper with a computer program.
S2.do: Keeps working as normal on the farm. Cuts small household costs like streaming and the phone deal, and plans to sell Tom's motorbike first if his delivery hours are cut.
S2.feel: Sorry for the office workers and safe for herself, with some guilt about feeling safe.
S2.quote: Nobody's sending a robot to scrape cubicles because of a computer program.
S2.fieldNote: She feels safest here, but the threat moved to her partner's delivery job, which showed how thin their household margin is. She was specific that his motorbike would be sold first. Her policy ideas are concrete: paid retraining funded by the companies that save money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be loud about it, to be honest. If house prices boom and shares boom, that's people who already own things getting richer. I'd say the gains should go to the people losing out, and to people like me who'll never own a house at this rate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What I really think is the cottage matters more than ever. If house prices go mad, I'll never get out of a tied house. I'll be Glen's tenant till I'm fifty, and if I ever fall out with him, I'm homeless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hang on tighter. I'd stop asking for a pay rise. I'd start putting a bit by every week, even twenty a week, into a tin, because the bank's no better than a tin. And I'd go with Tom to whatever protest there is in town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not about the cows, about the roof. It's a strange thing, to be safe at work and feel trapped by it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stop asking for a rise but go to protests. Those pull in different directions. How do you square that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know. At work I'd keep my mouth shut because Glen holds the keys to my house. Out in town, in a crowd, I'm not Glen's herd hand, I'm just someone who's angry. That's the only place I'd feel safe to say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the milk side look like in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If loads of people lose office jobs, they buy cheaper milk, the supermarket's own brand, and the dairy pays Glen even less. So physical jobs might be untouched, but the money in them isn't. That's what nobody in the news would say.

S3.say: I'd say loudly that the gains should go to the people losing out, not to people who already own houses and shares. People like me will never own a house at this rate.
S3.think: The tied cottage matters more than ever, because if house prices boom I can never leave it. I'd be Glen's tenant for decades, and homeless if I ever fell out with him.
S3.do: Stops asking for a pay rise and keeps quiet at work. Starts saving about twenty a week in a tin at home, and goes with Tom to protests in town.
S3.feel: Anxious about the roof over her head rather than the work itself. Safe in the job but trapped by it.
S3.quote: It's a strange thing, to be safe at work and feel trapped by it.
S3.fieldNote: The clearest say and think gap so far: loud in a crowd, silent at work, because her landlord is her boss. She noticed something the card left out, that falling office wages could push down milk prices. Her worry here is housing, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks for staying with me. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ban them, or tax them till it hurts. There'd have to be a union for farm workers with teeth, and I'd join that day. I'd be telling everyone online that this is what happens when nobody stops it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's already here for us. The farm two miles up has milking robots, big orange boxes the cows walk into on their own. Glen went to look at them last spring and came back quiet. The robot doesn't need the cottage. If the cows go to a machine, Tom and I go out the gate with the furniture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. That's the honest answer. I'd ask Glen straight out whether he's buying them, and I'd ask him to give me a year's warning. Then I'd look for anything with a house, and there's nothing round here, so probably Tom's mum's back bedroom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. Like the floor going. I'm not good with new things and I can't see a version where I'm the one running the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you see yourself learning to run the robots, the way some herd hands do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some can, the clever ones. I watched the lad up at the other farm with his laptop, looking at graphs of which cow went in when. I froze just watching. I'd try if Glen made me, but I'd be bad at it and we'd both know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Biscuit's generation of calves, if you had to leave?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's a daft question but I'll answer it. I'd say sorry I won't be there when you calve. Somebody will, or something will, and it won't know you followed me down the pen.

S4.say: I'd say ban the robots or tax them heavily, and I'd join a farm workers' union with real power the day it existed. Online I'd say this is what happens when nobody stops it.
S4.think: It's already arriving for us, because the farm up the road has milking robots and Glen came back quiet from seeing them. The robot doesn't need the cottage, so losing the job means losing our home.
S4.do: Asks the owner directly whether he's buying robots and asks for a year's warning. Looks for any job that comes with housing, and expects to end up in Tom's mother's back bedroom.
S4.feel: Sick and shaken, like the floor going. She can't picture herself running the machines.
S4.quote: The robot doesn't need the cottage. If the cows go to a machine, Tom and I go out the gate with the furniture.
S4.fieldNote: This was the only scenario where she ran out of plans; she said 'I don't know' before anything else. Milking robots aren't hypothetical to her, they're two miles away. She knows she's not the type to learn the new system and didn't pretend otherwise.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots one, the last one, because it's the only one where I lose the house and the job on the same day. What would help is a law that says a tied cottage can't be taken back for six months after the job goes, and a wage while you retrain. And a union. I keep saying union because nobody else will.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the cows. Everyone talks about whether the robots are good for business. Nobody asks whether the cows like them. Glen says the ones up the road are calmer. I don't know if that makes me feel better or worse.

headlineQuote: The robot doesn't need the cottage. If the cows go to a machine, Tom and I go out the gate with the furniture.
portrait: Uma Petrov is a 27-year-old herd hand on a 180-cow dairy, up at four every day and living with her partner Tom in a cottage that comes with the job. She knows she is still slow and below average, has about three weeks of savings, and has never used AI tools. Through the office scenarios she feels safe but squeezed, with her worries landing on Tom's delivery hours and on housing. In the robot scenario her fear becomes concrete, because a farm two miles away already milks with robots. Her answers return again and again to unions, paid retraining and protection for people in tied housing.
biggestWorry: The fast robots scenario, because milking robots could take her job and the tied cottage on the same day.
whatWouldHelp: A law giving workers six months in a tied cottage after a job ends, paid retraining, and a farm workers' union with real power.
